summary: The Open channel flow calculator turns the channel slope, the bottom width (b) and more into freeboard (F). It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Open channel flow calculator work?
sections.html:
The Open channel flow calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports freeboard (F) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the cross section, the design and the surface); then you type in the channel slope (s), the bottom width (b) (Channel specifications), the slope (z₁) (Channel specifications) and the top width (T) (Channel specifications).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Open channel flow calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Freeboard (F)=((1 ÷ 10) × water flow depth (y))
Cross-sectional area (A)=(bottom width (b) × water flow depth (y))
Cross-sectional area (A)=((1 ÷ 2) × water flow depth (y) × (2 × bottom width (b) + slope (z₁) × water flow depth (y) + slope (z₂) × water flow depth (y)))
Cross-sectional area (A)=((1 ÷ 2) × (water flow depth (y) ^ 2) × (slope (z₁) + slope (z₂)))
Cross-sectional area (A)=((radius ^ 2) × ((radius − water flow depth (y)) ÷ radius) − radius × the square root of (water flow depth (y) × (2 × radius − water flow depth (y))) + water flow depth (y) × the square root of (water flow depth (y) × (2 × radius − water flow depth (y))))
Wetted perimeter (P)=(bottom width (b) + 2 × water flow depth (y))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Open channel flow calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the channel slope, the bottom width (b) and the slope (z₁) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Open channel flow calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns freeboard (F), derived from the channel slope, the bottom width (b) and the slope (z₁). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Open channel flow calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the channel slope, the bottom width (b), the slope (z₁) and the top width (T), which is 11 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter channel slope (s) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Channel slope (s) opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Manning's coefficient (n) = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Open channel flow calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
